judgment is vacated, and the case is remanded to the United
States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit for further
consideration in light of Keathley v. Buddy Ayers Construction,
Inc., 608 U. S. 647 (2026).

pauperis and the petition for a writ of certiorari are granted.
The judgment is vacated, and the case is remanded to the United
States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit for further
consideration in light of Hunter v. United States, 608 U. S. 713
(2026).

Statement of SOTOMAYOR, J.
SUPREME COURT OF THE UNITED STATES
JESUS HERRERA-SALAZAR v. UNITED STATES
ON PETITION FOR WRIT OF CERTIORARI TO THE UNITED
STATES COURT OF APPEALS FOR THE TENTH CIRCUIT
No. 25–6989. Decided October 13, 2026
The petition for a writ of certiorari is denied.
Statement of JUSTICE SOTOMAYOR, with whom JUSTICE
GORSUCH joins, respecting the denial of certiorari.
Jesus Herrera-Salazar was indicted in 2020 on one count
of being “found in” the United States following removal, in
violation of 8 U. S. C. §1326(a). He pleaded guilty and
served his term of imprisonment. While on supervised re-
lease, during which he was expressly instructed not to leave
the Eastern District of Oklahoma, Herrera-Salazar was
pulled over in a traffic stop in Heavener, Oklahoma, and
once again arrested and indicted under §1326(a). He was
convicted by a jury and sentenced to new terms of impris-
onment and supervised release. Because I hope the facts of
this case are anomalous and because Herrera-Salazar has
since been removed from the United States, I concur in the
Court’s decision not to grant review in this case. I write,
however, to underscore the serious constitutional problems
that plague the Government’s treatment of Herrera-Salazar.
After being once convicted and punished for being found
in the United States and, as part of his original sentence,
prohibited from leaving the United States, Herrera-Salazar
was convicted and punished for being found in the United
States a second time. As an initial matter, it is not clear
that the statutory language “found in . . . the United States”
can fairly be read to encompass a person who has already
been found by the Government and compelled to remain in
the United States under Government supervision. Even as-
suming that it can, however, Herrera-Salazar’s second
2 HERRERA-SALAZAR v. UNITED STATES
Statement of SOTOMAYOR, J.
conviction is difficult to square with the Constitution’s ad-
monition that no person shall “be subject for the same of-
fence to be twice put in jeopardy of life or limb.” Amdt. 5.
As our precedents explain, “the Double Jeopardy Clause
protects against a second prosecution for the same offense
after conviction.” Currier v. Virginia, 585 U. S. 493, 501
(2018) (internal quotation marks omitted). The question in
a case like this is what constitutes the “same offense.”
In rejecting Herrera-Salazar’s double jeopardy objections,
the Tenth Circuit looked to the text of §1326(a) to answer
that question. It concluded that because the “ ‘allowable unit
of prosecution’ ” did not require a separate predicate reentry
for each violation of the statute, see Sanabria v. United
States, 437 U. S. 54, 69 (1978), each of Herrera-Salazar’s
prosecutions and convictions was for a separate offense. By
those lights, with a single unlawful reentry supplying the
necessary statutory predicate, a person in Herrera-Sala-
zar’s shoes can be subjected to repeated, limitless “found in”
charges without offending the Constitution.
“The Double Jeopardy Clause is not such a fragile guar-
antee that prosecutors can avoid its limitations by the sim-
ple expedient of dividing a single crime into a series of tem-
poral or spatial units.” Brown v. Ohio, 432 U. S. 161, 169
(1977). Yet that is just what the Government did here.
Herrera-Salazar was convicted of “a crime which was con-
tinuous, extending over the whole period” he was present in
the United States after his previous removal and reentry.
In re Nielsen, 131 U. S. 176, 187 (1889). That continuous
crime plainly could not have concluded until the Govern-
ment allowed Herrera-Salazar to leave the country. Be-
cause the crime of being found in the United States was
thus still ongoing at the time of his second arrest, the Gov-
ernment’s theory rests on the premise that Herrera-Salazar
could be charged, convicted, and punished twice solely “be-
cause the charges against him focused on different parts of ”
his compelled continuous presence in the United States.
3Cite as: 610 U. S. ____ (2026)
Statement of SOTOMAYOR, J.
Brown, 432 U. S., at 169 (recognizing a double jeopardy vi-
olation where the petitioner faced two charges based on two
points of time within a continuous “9-day joyride”).
When a defendant is convicted of a crime that involves
continuous, uninterrupted conduct, our precedents and the
logic of the Double Jeopardy Clause strongly suggest that
the Government is barred from charging that defendant
with the same continuous crime for a second time simply by
focusing on a different time marker. That makes sense.
Were it otherwise, there might be “ ‘an indictment covering
each of the . . . months’ ” of the continuous crime, “ ‘or even
an indictment covering every week.’ ” In re Nielsen, 131
U. S., at 186. There is even more force to this double jeop-
ardy objection where the Government itself effectively for-
bids the defendant to cease his unlawful conduct. Here, in-
deed, the Government might have charged Herrera-Salazar
with a separate violation of §1326(a) for each day that he
was “found in” prison while serving his sentence for the first
conviction. Absurd as that seems, it is a logical outgrowth
of the Government’s contention that Herrera-Salazar’s sec-
ond §1326(a) conviction poses no double jeopardy problem.
* * *
From the moment he was released from custody after
serving his first term of imprisonment, Herrera-Salazar
was presented with a Hobson’s choice. In the Government’s
eyes, whether Herrera-Salazar remained in the Eastern
District of Oklahoma or left the United States, he would be
breaking the law. While Herrera-Salazar was caught in
this bind, the Government prosecuted and punished him
yet again for being “found in” the United States, even
though all agree he was forbidden to leave the United
States. Should circumstances like these arise again, I en-
courage courts to avoid the constitutional absurdity that oc-
curred here and give the Double Jeopardy Clause its full
weight and meaning.
